source.title: Optimizing Mode Connectivity via Neuron Alignment
source.authors: N. Joseph Tatro; Pin-Yu Chen; Payel Das; Igor Melnyk; Prasanna Sattigeri; Rong-Jie Lai

record.tranche_reason: Measures activation correspondence between independently initialized, same-architecture networks using neuron alignment, and compares alignment methods; this is a different method from the original convergence studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports layer-wise activation-correlation comparisons and comparisons of curve performance under different alignment methods. Figure 1 and Figure 2 values are shown only in plots; the text describes their direction. Curve-accuracy results in Table 1 and robust-curve results are not included as separate rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions' representation similarity or convergence.
record.test_reason: Figure 1a reports a measurement bearing on V3. It shows the mean correlation of units in seed-different, same-architecture networks before and after correlation-based Hungarian matching, the same method as Li et al. (an original source). The rest of the paper uses alignment as a tool for mode connectivity and reports curve accuracy, which is T4-like. The V3 evidence is therefore thin and figure-only.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that neuron alignment approximates a nearly locally optimal weight permutation, yields better and faster-trained low-loss curves between networks, makes intermediate activations along the curve more similar to the endpoints, and largely removes the robust loss barrier between adversarially trained models.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses activation-based neuron alignment and mode-connectivity curves between same-architecture models; it does not reproduce the original studies' methods for convergence across networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported performance of learned curves depends on the alignment technique: post-activation alignment performs better than pre-activation alignment, and cross-correlation performs better than the other compared methods.

fits_no_version.finding: For CIFAR100 models, the computed alignment permutation was identical whether 2,500, 5,000 or 10,000 training images were used.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron matching between seed-different networks is stable with respect to the size of the in-distribution input subset used to compute it.

fits_no_version.finding: Curves between models are higher-accuracy when endpoints are permutation-aligned (Table 1), with larger gains for narrow networks such as TinyTen. Post-activation cross-correlation alignment beats pre-activation L2 alignment (Fig 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Permutation symmetry, not lack of shared structure, accounts for much of the loss barrier between independently trained networks.

record.problems: The convergence evidence is limited to same-architecture image classifiers and activation alignment. Figure 1 and Figure 2 results are plot-only in the supplied text, and the Figure 1 network-pair architecture and dataset are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1, Table 2, Figures 3–9, and other curve and robust-accuracy results are omitted because they report curve performance or robustness rather than representation similarity or convergence named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: No scale sweep; no cross-architecture, cross-objective or cross-data comparison.
No shared-subspace analysis. No quantitative fraction of matched features. No per-architecture or per-dataset breakdown of the correlation signature.
Permutation alignment is used for curve finding; mapping loss, stitching and relative representations are not evaluated.
No interpretable features or circuits compared.
No comparison of similarity measures, settings or OOD inputs for measuring convergence. The alignment-method comparison is by curve accuracy only.
No test of plateau or of causes of convergence.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a mode-connectivity paper. Its only direct convergence evidence is Fig 1a, a reuse of Li et al.'s correlation matching, shown without numbers. Six seeds are trained per architecture and dataset (3 pairs), but the text does not say which pairs Fig 1a aggregates. The record's V6 labels are dropped: rows R4–R6 compare the study's own alignment methods by downstream curve accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model scale or capability, and no comparison across different architectures, objectives, data or modalities as a test of convergence with scale.
No paired image-caption data or vision-language models.
Tests same-architecture image classifiers trained with different random initializations; does not test shared subspaces or whether individual units or bases recur.

Although the method permutes weights to align neurons, the paper does not test whether one model's representation can be mapped to another with little loss, or compare stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
No interpretable features, SAE features, neurons as semantic features, or circuits are identified and compared across models.
Compares alignment techniques and their resulting curve accuracy, but does not systematically vary similarity-measure settings such as neighbour count or test out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not test whether alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives cause convergence rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: network pairs (aggregate; architecture not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean cross-correlation of corresponding units before and after neuron alignment.

conditions.value: mean and standard deviation over a set of different network pairs

rows.measure: Mean cross-correlation between corresponding units at each layer
rows.value: After alignment, correspondence quality at each layer is improved; exact values are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over network pairs is displayed; exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes increased correlation after alignment and says the method matches a subset of highly correlated features. The architecture and dataset for this aggregate figure are not stated.
rows.check: Subject is unspecified: the text never states the architecture or dataset behind Fig 1a. Values are plot-only. The text says matching recovers 'a subset of highly correlated features', which fits V3's 'many features, not identical units'.

rows.subject: midpoint of unaligned learned curves
rows.operation_detail: Compared the midpoint's layer-wise activation-correlation signature with endpoint models, before and after aligning the midpoint to an endpoint.

conditions.value: before and after alignment to endpoint

rows.measure: Cross-correlation signature between endpoint models and curve midpoint
rows.value: The unaligned curve midpoint is described as mostly aligned to the endpoints; exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The text reports that the midpoint is mostly aligned even when the curve endpoints are not aligned.
rows.check: The curve midpoint is a model optimised along a curve between the endpoints, not an independently initialised network, so this row does not measure convergent learning across seeds.

rows.subject: midpoint of aligned learned curves
rows.operation_detail: Compared the midpoint's layer-wise activation-correlation signature with endpoint models, before and after aligning the midpoint to an endpoint.

conditions.value: before and after alignment to endpoint

rows.measure: Cross-correlation signature between endpoint models and curve midpoint
rows.value: After alignment, the midpoint and endpoint correlation signatures are described as almost identical; exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The paper states that neuron alignment promotes greater similarity of intermediate activations.
rows.check: Same issue as R2. Similarity of an aligned-curve midpoint to an endpoint is a product of the study's curve method, not independent convergence.

rows.subject: TinyTen
rows.operation_detail: Compared test accuracy along curves produced by different activation-alignment techniques.

conditions.value: different techniques, including pre- and post-activation alignment and cross-correlation

rows.value: The alignment methods outperform the unaligned case; post-activation alignment outperforms pre-activation alignment, and maximizing cross-correlation outperforms the other methods. Exact values are figure only.
rows.note: This compares alignment choices by their effect on curve test accuracy, rather than directly comparing multiple similarity measures of representation convergence.
rows.check: This compares the study's own alignment variants by curve test accuracy. That is method performance, not a test of how measured representational convergence depends on the similarity metric.

relationships.condition: Same-architecture image classifiers trained from different random seeds (architecture and dataset for Fig 1a unstated)
relationships.reason: After matching, layer-wise correlation of corresponding units rises markedly. The authors describe this as matching a subset of highly correlated features (R1). Figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Matching markedly increased corresponding-unit correlations across layers, revealing a subset of highly correlated features.
